skyline.text: Why the best people need other excellent people around them
Why playing at statehood is no training for coercive power
Amit Varma’s cure for writer’s block: two or three essays

brief.head: Still rolling
brief.text: There are no film cans any more, but the producer still says “rolling”. Conventions like the QWERTY keyboard, Amit Varma said, stick long after their reasons vanish. {008-C01}

brief.head: Capital follows talent
brief.text: Open, diverse cities draw entrepreneurs, artists and gay and lesbian communities, Varma said, citing Richard Florida. Capital then chases that talent, and a virtuous cycle begins. {008-C05}

brief.head: Why do they leave?
brief.text: IIT graduates who go abroad are making rational choices, Varma argued. The real question is why India chases good people away instead of building centres of excellence. {008-C08}

brief.head: A deep bench
brief.text: Want a cute 20-man team? Finland will do, Ajay Shah said. Want 2,000 people? Come to India, where the depth of the bench is phenomenal. {008-C09}

brief.head: Guns make bad states
brief.text: Freedom won by armed struggle tends to go badly, Shah said, because violence lifts generals, not philosopher kings. India’s one piece of magic was ahimsa. {008-C14}

thought.text: The company we keep actually shapes who we are.
thought.who: Amit Varma, on the looking-glass self and why he likes to sit with Ajay Shah

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on where talent flourishes
lead.head: Genius loves company
body: Amit Varma once turned down a Nobel laureate. When Abhijit Banerjee won the prize, his publishers offered him for Varma’s podcast that same week, but for only one hour. Varma asked for at least two. When they refused, he said no. {008-S01}

One hour, he reasoned, would have got him the standard questions about RCTs. Three would have let him go back to the 1960s, when his father studied at Presidency College under Banerjee’s father, Deepak Banerjee.
The story led to a column on this episode’s question: why does talent gather in a few places, software engineers in Silicon Valley, filmmakers in Bombay?
Banerjee went to Presidency College, then JNU, then Harvard. Varma’s controversial claim was that Harvard was critical to his development.
## The ten-dollar lesson
His evidence was Michael Kremer’s 1993 paper on the O-ring, the $10 part whose failure destroyed the $3.2 billion Challenger shuttle in 1986.
In complex work, Varma explained, quality multiplies rather than adds. Ten people at 0.99 produce 9.05; at 0.95, 5.99; at 0.90, just 3.49. {008-C02}
“So a small difference in talent leads to a massive difference in output and productivity,” he said. The best people therefore gain most by working beside each other.

Ajay Shah agreed, with caveats. Where parts are standardised, as in a car or in software, people can work apart. The hard part is agreeing who does what: “The contracting is a bigger problem than the actual work.” {008-C04}
## Lost geniuses
Shah also thought Indian middle-class parents overstate how make-or-break clusters are. Ramanujan, cut off in a remote corner of Tamil Nadu, rebuilt 19th-century mathematics on his own.

Varma answered with Viswanathan Anand, who conquered a chess world dominated by the Soviet school without its training. It was, he said, “like someone taking a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race and winning the damn thing”. {008-S06}
But outliers inspire; they do not make policy. “There are countless Ramanujans and Anands who have been lost to us who are unseen,” Varma said.
Clusters can also corrupt. Bombay, he said, can take bright small-town kids steeped in culture and, within a year, flatten them into shallow party talk.
## A state in rehearsal
The second half turned to the state. In McLeod Ganj, Shah walked through the Central Tibetan Administration, a government in exile funded by donations, with no taxation and no coercive power.
Could it be training wheels for a free Tibet? No, he argued: nobody learns to wield coercive power by play-acting. {008-C13}

India, he said, should build regulators as patiently as it builds bridges, with design, processes and staged powers, rather than notifying a law and expecting a handful of people to perform overnight.

Varma was gloomier. India’s state, he said, was designed to rule rather than serve, a continuation of the colonial one. Independent India, he pointed out, taxed salt far more than the British Empire had.

Shah’s reply was hope as an intellectual project. A century ago, he said, India’s chattering classes argued over what free India would look like, and got the state wrong. Now is the time for research.
Varma, for his part, said the theory explained why he spends so much time with Shah: “That’s why I like to sit with you, because it can only make me a better thinker and a better person.”

second.label: Physics at Göttingen
second.head: Bad apple, top class
second.deck: Amit Varma on how Göttingen took an unhappy misfit to another level
body: At school and college, Oppenheimer was unhappy and fitted in nowhere. He even tried to poison his physics teacher, Amit Varma said, by putting poison in an apple. {008-S03}
Then he went to the University of Göttingen. He was taught by Max Born, who, Varma said, coined the term quantum mechanics. His classmates were of the calibre of Dirac and John von Neumann.

For Varma, it was the O-ring theory at work in a single life: among peers of the highest calibre, the misfit went to an entirely different level. If you are lucky in a particular place and time, he said, a congregation can produce “an exponential explosion of talent”. {#gottingen}

quote.text: He has classmates of the calibre of Dirac and John von Neumann, and he goes to an entirely different level.

second.caption: Oppenheimer at Göttingen

third.head: Comrades out, brokers in
body: In Warsaw, Ajay Shah heard a story. After communism ended, Poland took the office of the Communist Party, the biggest and most powerful building in the city, and turned it into the stock exchange. {008-S10}
“They were making a statement that we are finished with this stuff and we now want to learn to be a capitalist country,” Shah said.

Having lived under communism and knowing how bad it was, Eastern Europeans wanted to run far from it, he argued. Joining the European Union helped too: it came with 20,000 pages of draft laws and treaty restrictions. {#eu}

Russia, by contrast, privatised companies and asked markets to appear overnight, with Jeff Sachs among those pushing, but paid too little attention to the state. “Freedom is coded into laws and state institutions,” Shah said. {008-C15}

p2.title: The case for clusters
p2.deck: Amit Varma on why talent congregates, Ajay Shah on why statecraft can’t be rehearsed, and both on Orwell

sections.label: The first idea
sections.head: Small gaps, giant sums
sections.caption: the O-ring theory of talent
body: In 1986 the space shuttle Challenger, a $3.2 billion project, exploded because a $10 O-ring failed. Michael Kremer named his seminal 1993 paper after that flimsy part, and Amit Varma built his case on it. {008-S02}
The lesson, Varma said, is not the trivial point that a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. It is about the interplay between talent, productivity and wages.
In complex work, quality multiplies. Ten people each performing at 0.99 produce an output of 9.05. At 0.95, itself incredibly talented, the output falls to 5.99. At 0.90 it is just 3.49. {008-C02}
## Worth twice the money

So someone at 0.99 can be paid twice or thrice as much as someone at 0.95, though the gap barely shows. The effect is strongest, Varma said, where quality matters more than quantity, since one great novelist beats three mediocre ones, and where a task has thousands of links that must all hold.

That is why the best people seek each other out, and why Harvard mattered to Abhijit Banerjee. Elite colleges do offer credentials and sorting, Varma granted. But they also put you among some of the finest minds.
~ For a fuller account, he pointed to Tyler Cowen’s Marginal Revolution University video on the model, which he called fantastic. {#cowen}

quote.text: You need to be around other staggeringly talented and qualified people to get a full expression of your abilities.

sections.label: The rejoinder
sections.head: Trust first, work anywhere
sections.caption: plug compatibility and trust
body: Ajay Shah came at the O-ring problem from the factory floor. Mass manufacturing, he said, solved it with standardised parts. A car contains 10,000 parts and works flawlessly because every ball bearing sits within very tight tolerances. {#car}

Software does the same with APIs. “That damn thing had better just work,” Shah said. Where the interface is defined, two people need never talk. A movie is the opposite: hundreds of people in imprecise, poorly defined relationships. {008-C03}

Distance from a cluster is no death sentence either. Cut off in a remote corner of Tamil Nadu, Ramanujan set about rebuilding the mathematics of the 19th century on his own. The early University of Chicago, far from the East Coast, bred independent thinking. {008-S05}
## The handshake problem

The real limit, Shah argued, is contracting: agreeing who does what, how decisions are made and how resources are shared. That needs people who know and trust each other, which is the magic of London, New York and Cambridge, Massachusetts. After that, the work can happen anywhere. {008-C04}
~ In the humanities and social sciences, he added, “authenticity is king”. {008-C07} To know Indian economics you must be in India; abroad, he felt “a certain emptiness”.

quote.text: I will suggest that the contracting is a bigger problem than the actual work.

sections.label: Training wheels
sections.head: No taxes, no training
sections.caption: the government in exile
body: Ajay Shah’s T-shirt bore the name of the Tibet Museum in McLeod Ganj, which he called a really great museum. It sits inside the complex of the Central Tibetan Administration: “a living, breathing government in exile”. {008-S09}

Shah was proud that India has been kind to Tibetan refugees, even when it was costly. But the CTA, with its Department of Finance and Department of Home, runs on donations. It has no taxation and no coercive power.

Could this wannabe state be training wheels for a free Tibet? Shah thought not. “Coercive power is a poison,” he said, and play-acting is no preparation. Tidy departments might even lull people into “isomorphic mimicry”. {008-C13}
## How new states fare
When Charles de Gaulle led the French government in exile in London, Shah doubted he set up a department of health; he focused on getting to a free France. {#degaulle}

New states, Shah said, have mostly fared badly, worst where freedom came through armed struggle. The success stories are in Eastern Europe. For China, the best hope is the institutional DNA of Taiwan, not the CTA.
~ Amit Varma found the play-acting admirable but poignant: ministries that could not possibly look like those of an actual free Tibet.

quote.text: You don’t develop state capability without actually fighting with the battle of the evil that is coercive power.

sections.label: The Indian lesson
sections.head: Regulators are bridges too
sections.caption: building a regulator like a bridge
body: India, Ajay Shah said, accepts that a bridge takes time: project management, many hands, and a minister cutting the ribbon two or five years later. “But nobody expects a zero day lag between the decision to have a bridge and the bridge.” {008-C16}

A new regulator, such as a food safety authority, deserves the same patience: organisational design, written processes, trained staff, IT systems and repeated review of checks and balances, with powers notified in stages. Launched overnight, it goes into firefighting from day three and never recovers.

The closest India came, he said, was the plan MS Sahoo and Ravi Narain led for the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India. “In reality, the law was notified and overnight five people were expected to perform.” {008-S11}
## Is decay inevitable?

Amit Varma asked whether all institutions must degrade. No, Shah said. An institution’s DNA lies in its law, and coercive power, like a nuclear reactor, needs enough cladding. “Most of our Indian laws are based on an optimistic reading of human beings.” {008-C17}
~ The usual Indian response to a failing agency, he said, is to demand a better CEO, a primitive great man theory. The real debate should be over checks and balances. {008-C18}

quote.text: So we are in that R&D phase of figuring out what a successful, prosperous India would look like.

sections.label: Amit’s pick
sections.head: Write clearly, think better
sections.caption: Orwell and clear writing
body: Amit Varma’s recommendation was not *Animal Farm* or *1984* but George Orwell’s collected essays, which present his work in chronological order: a look at Orwell the thinker. {008-R15}
Whenever he got stuck on a column, Varma said, he would read two or three pieces, whatever their subject. The clarity of Orwell’s language and the rhythms he builds “would free something within me”.
## Writing is research

Writing and thinking feed each other both ways, he argued. “If you force yourself to write clearly, you are forced to think better because you cannot hide behind abstract words or vague jargon.” {008-C20}

He cited Joan Didion: “I don’t know what I think until I write it down.” {#didion} Deirdre McCloskey, whose *Economical Writing* he also recommended, holds, in his paraphrase, that the writing is research.

Ajay Shah recommended a story about the novelist Cormac McCarthy cleaning up a scientific paper, and recited from memory lines of a poem Orwell slipped into an essay. “Insane memory,” said Varma. {008-J20}

~ Shah’s own pick built on the O-ring talk: William Easterly’s *The Elusive Quest for Growth*, which knocks the faddish ideas out of development. {008-R22} Varma added Easterly’s *The White Man’s Burden*.

quote.text: Saints should always be judged guilty until they are proved innocent
quote.who: George Orwell, as read by Amit Varma

side.boxText: Michael Kremer shared the Nobel with Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo. His seminal 1993 paper, *The O-Ring Theory of Economic Development*, explains with simple multiplication why small differences in skill create huge differences in output and pay. {008-R02}

contQuote.text: The question then is that why are they having to go abroad? What can we do to create centres of excellence here so that people feel inspired, people feel happy?

stories.caption: Anand and the Soviet school
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Viswanathan Anand and the Soviet school
stories.head: The boy who skipped Soviet school
body: Some time in the 1930s, as Amit Varma guessed, a top Soviet functionary named Nikolai Krylenko demanded “shock brigades of chess players” and “a five-year plan for chess”. He could not have said it later, Varma noted: Stalin purged him in 1938. {#krylenko}

The Soviet Union wanted to prove its superiority through a game of the brain. Chess was taught in schools the way maths is, giving a huge pool from which talent was trained systematically up to grandmaster level. The Soviet school came to mean a shared way of thinking, heuristics handed from trainer to pupil.

Varma’s friend Devangshu Datta, who played serious chess for India in the 1980s, likened facing East Europeans to pitting self-taught HSC-level maths students against postgraduates. In the post-mortem, the opponent would explain that his trainer had taught him how to play that structure. “And you’d be like, shit.” {008-J06}
Ajay Shah supplied the chess world’s inside joke for that gap: “as every Russian schoolboy knows”. {008-J15}

Into this world came Viswanathan Anand. In his formative years, in the Philippines as Varma recalls it, a TV chess programme set puzzles. Anand kept sending the right answers until, Varma remembers, they asked him to stop entering and offered him all the chess books he wanted. {008-J05}

Without Soviet training, Anand rose to dominate and later became world champion. “The metaphor I draw for it is like someone taking a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race and winning the damn thing,” Varma said. {008-S06}
~ Yet Varma calls Anand an outlier, not a model: for every Ramanujan or Anand who made it, countless others were lost.
stories.why: A system that gathers and trains talent builds a store of knowledge that a lone genius must rebuild from scratch. That makes Anand’s feat staggering, and makes him an exception to admire rather than a policy to copy. {008-C06}
stories.postscript: Varma’s other image for it: “like winning Wimbledon today with a wooden racket”.

stories.start: But I think of Bollywood as yes, a place of great opportunity
stories.end: And this guy will be like, Dude, how are you doing? Let's go chill.
stories.caption: Bombay’s shallow end
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what Bombay does to small-town talent
stories.head: Big city, small talk
body: Bollywood, Amit Varma said, is a place of great opportunity, but Bombay is also “where dreams come to die and art comes to be corrupted”. {008-S07}
On an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, Vikram Sathaye told him about bright kids from small towns in Maharashtra who arrive steeped in culture, reading Vijay Tendulkar, deep into local forms.

In Bombay they meet shallow people. A year later, Sathaye runs into one of them at a party, someone who had discussed Tendulkar with him the year before. Now it is: “Dude, how are you doing? Let’s go chill.”

~ Ajay Shah countered that 99% of everything is crass and shallow, in Bollywood or Silicon Valley alike. Varma’s point was different: a good person can come to Bollywood and produce bad work because there are “incentives for mediocrity”. {008-C12}
stories.why: Clusters do not only lift talent up. Their incentives and status games can also flatten it, and the pressure to fit in can strip away what made a small-town newcomer distinctive.

stories.start: there is a counterforce to this you know I did an episode
stories.end: They had a big round of funding last year, and it's phenomenal.
stories.caption: the reverse migration
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Vinay Singhal’s streaming bet
stories.head: Haryanvi kids come home
body: Vinay Singhal described his app, Stage.in, to Amit Varma as Netflix for Bharat: not in languages like Hindi or Punjabi but in dialects, Haryanvi, Bhojpuri and, Varma thinks, now Rajasthani.

Traditional venture capitalists told him it would never work. He charged Netflix rates anyway and has, Varma thinks, some 300,000 subscribers by now. {#subscribers} The VCs are flocking, and there was a big funding round last year.

Singhal also described what he called the reverse migration from Bollywood. {008-S08} Haryanvi kids who once headed to Bombay to make films are coming back, to a Haryanvi film industry of some 3,000 people. {#haryanvi}

~ Cities drive human progress, Varma said, but they homogenise: a Bhojpuri speaker in a Hindi city may drop the dialect to avoid seeming “vernie”. Technology and capitalism can now push the other way.

quote.text: One of the side effects is that homogenisation happens, you can lose dialects, you can lose subcultures.

stories.start: my good friend Ahim Zaileis is a statistician in Vienna
stories.end: and we were able to do very interesting things
stories.caption: a paper written by strangers
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on research across borders
stories.head: Strangers on a mailing list
body: Ajay Shah’s good friend Achim Zeileis is a statistician in Vienna. Shah, Ila Patnaik and Zeileis struck up a conversation over mailing lists and realised they were chasing different pieces of a correlated puzzle. {008-S04}
They wrote a paper together, one Shah counts among the nice papers of his life, without ever meeting. “We got all the way to our first paper without even video calls, just on email and SVN,” he said.
Only later did they meet, and it was great. Their paper *What is the New Chinese Currency Regime?* is among Shah’s recommendations.

~ Still, Shah said, remote teams need human rapport. Without meeting, humour is “so dangerous it can just be misunderstood”, or everyone turns into automatons writing “horrible ChatGPT language”. {#humour}
stories.why: Serious research can be done at internet scale once the work is defined. What still needs a room, Shah argued, is the trust that lets people agree who does what. {008-C04}
